title: Expense Fraud

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Expense fraud covers false, inflated, or duplicate expense claims, personal costs submitted as business expenses, and collusion between employees, approvers, or vendors. In the AI Accountant context, this page addresses detection and forensic review across corporate card transactions, travel and entertainment spend, invoices, and receipt submissions. The focus is on patterns that indicate deliberate misuse rather than simple policy mistakes, and on evidence that can support an investigation.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Detection systems run on data drawn from expense management platforms, ERP systems, corporate card feeds, and scanned or photographed receipts. Receipt images are processed with optical character recognition to extract merchant, date, amount, and line-item detail. Models typically operate in batch or near real time within a cloud or on-premises environment, feeding alerts into case management tools used by audit and compliance teams.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work combines rule-based checks with machine learning models that learn normal spending behavior for each employee, role, department, and vendor category. Common techniques include anomaly detection on amounts and frequencies, duplicate receipt matching, merchant category mismatch analysis, and network analysis to spot shared addresses, bank accounts, or approver relationships. Outputs are ranked risk scores and supporting evidence, which human investigators then review before any finding is finalized.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Expense fraud detection raises direct questions about employee privacy, data protection, and the legal basis for monitoring personal spending patterns. Organizations must manage false positives carefully, keep clear audit trails of model inputs and decisions, and ensure that any evidence used in disciplinary action is explainable and reproducible. Retention limits, works council or labor law requirements, and rules on automated decision-making all shape how these systems can be deployed, and this page describes common practice rather than offering legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward continuous monitoring and pre-approval risk scoring, where a claim is assessed before payment rather than after the fact. Generative AI is being explored to draft plain-language explanations of why a claim was flagged and to summarize evidence for investigators. Tighter integration with travel booking, receipt capture, and vendor master data is expected to reduce manual review and shorten the time from submission to resolution.
